item.title: China, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand launch 171st joint Mekong patrol amid cross-border crime challenges
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25 20:25:00
Chinese law enforcement officers take part in the joint patrol operation along the Mekong River. Photo: CCTV News A joint patrol involving law enforcement authorities from China, Laos, Myanmar and Thailand is in full swing along the Mekong River this week, as the four countries step up efforts to combat cross-border crimes such as drug trafficking, illegal border crossings and smuggling. The 171st joint patrol operation began on Sunday, with three Chinese law enforcement vessels departing from Jingha Police Wharf in the Xishuangbanna Dai autonomous prefecture, Southwest China's Yunnan Province, according to state broadcaster CCTV. Commanders from the four countries boarded Chinese vessel No.53108, which is serving as the fleet's command center for the operation. Law enforcement vessels from Laos and Myanmar respectively departed from Mengmo in Laos and Wanbang in Myanmar. After conducting separate patrols along designated sections, the vessels are expected to meet at a predetermined location to form a joint fleet, CCTV said. The operation will combine full-route joint patrols, section-based cruises and coordinated ground-river enforcement. Teams are expected to inspect key waterways, riverside ports and ferry crossings, targeting drug trafficking, illegal border crossings, cross-border smuggling and other criminal activities, while identifying potential safety hazards, according to CCTV. The four countries will also hold a multilateral information-exchange meeting to share updates on security conditions along the river, assess emerging criminal trends and discuss closer cooperation in intelligence-sharing, case investigations and joint prevention measures. China will rotate personnel stationed at two joint patrol liaison points in Mengmo and Ban Xiangguo in Laos. Chinese law enforcement officers will also visit relevant departments in Laos, Myanmar and Thailand to discuss practical cooperation to combat crime along the Mekong River and the China-Laos Railway, according to the report. The latest operation comes as transnational criminal networks continue to pose challenges to security in the Mekong subregion, particularly in drug production and trafficking. The Mekong River, which is known as the Lancang River in China, is an important transportation route connecting countries in the region. Its cross-border nature means that criminal activities can extend beyond the jurisdiction of any single country, making information-sharing and coordinated enforcement particularly important. The Thai Office of the Narcotics Control Board has also identified the Mekong as a trafficking route for illicit drugs from the Golden Triangle and the upper Mekong to countries further downstream. Its "Safe Mekong" cooperation framework emphasizes that drug production and trafficking in the region cannot be addressed by one country acting alone. The four-country joint patrol mechanism was established in December 2011, following a deadly attack on two cargo ships on the Mekong River in October of that year, in which 13 Chinese sailors were killed. The incident exposed serious security challenges facing commercial shipping in the region and prompted the four countries to strengthen coordinated law enforcement. Since then, the mechanism has developed beyond vessel patrols to include joint command arrangements, intelligence exchanges, emergency response coordination and law enforcement training.

item.title: Chinese humanoid robot maker, funds pledge at least 1b yuan for industry partners
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25 18:33:00
A humanoid robot demonstrates how to scoop popcorn into a container at EngineAI's 2026 World Developer Conference in Shenzhen, South China's Guangdong Province, on November 25, 2026. Photo: Tao Mingyang/Global Times Chinese humanoid robot maker EngineAI announced on Wednesday that it will work with industry funds to provide at least 1 billion yuan ($210 million) in support for partners developing commercial applications. Industry analysts said that opening robot platforms to more developers can accelerate breakthroughs in humanoid robotics, while collecting different users' problems and experiences, creating what the industry called "a two-way exchange." Zhao Tongyang, EngineAI's founder and CEO, announced the plan at the company's 2026 World Developer Conference in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, on Wednesday. The company outlined its CoRun approach to sharing development work across teams and its Engine Plan for developing partners. The fund will support joint projects involving technology companies, universities and research institutes, Zhao said. Investment would give the partners a long-term stake in each other's success. As more applications come into use, the operating data they generate could help developers improve the machines and attract more partners, he said. "Some of you have brought code and want to try it on a real machine," Zhao said, adding that others already have a working product and are looking for their first customers. EngineAI would offer engineering support and access to robots, data and computing resources. Once a partner has an application to demonstrate, the company can introduce it to customers facing the same problem. Zhao also described how partners had already found different jobs for the same hardware. Duolun Technology used EngineAI's T800 and PM01 platforms to develop applications for directing traffic, teaching road safety and helping students get to school safely, he said. At a Luxshare Precision factory in Suzhou, East China's Jiangsu Province, the T800 was connected to the plant's management system so it could receive an order, navigate to a pickup point, collect materials and deliver them. Shi Fan, an assistant professor in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the National University of Singapore, said that he saw a parallel with open-source development at Chinese AI companies. In his own field, researchers already use open-source tools "to control robots, train them and get them to keep learning." Sharing those tools allows more teams to build on existing work and expands the community familiar with the manufacturer's platform, he said. Even with 1 billion or 10 billion yuan, a single manufacturer would struggle to develop applications across so many industries on its own, Li Qinglin, a representative of TurkeyBro, an engineer resource community targeting embodied AI, told the Global Times. "What humanoid robots lack most right now are real-world applications," Pan Wenqiang, a representative of robot software developer Flykor, told the Global Times. The company specializes in adapting robots for particular uses and works with several manufacturers, including EngineAI, Unitree Robotics and AgiBot. Pan said that cooperation was more efficient than companies working alone because each application depends on businesses at several stages: manufacturers supply the machines, developers adapt the software for the job, and service providers keep the robots working after delivery. Other Chinese manufacturers are opening up different parts of the development process, too. Unitree provides a Python interface that developers can use to run software on its G1 and H1 humanoids. AgiBot has released data from real robots, including expert demonstrations and human corrections during operation. It has also announced plans to work with the OpenAtom Foundation on common technical interfaces and joint testing for humanoids. At the APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen on November 17, Unitree founder Wang Xingxing said that recent advances suggested a tipping point could come soon, the 21st Century Business Herald reported. Wang offered a more specific timeframe at the World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit on November 4, saying that 2027 would likely mark a tipping point for the robotics industry and its AI models, according to the Securities Times. Asked whether an open ecosystem could bring a breakthrough closer, Shi said, "I think it will definitely speed things up." Each new use gives developers a chance to identify a problem and work with the manufacturer to resolve it, he said.

item.title: A Chinese man's enduring dedication to forest
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25 12:35:00
Xie Peng points at a digital monitoring platform at the Fengyu state-owned ecological forest farm in Xi'an, northwest China's Shaanxi Province, on Nov. 5, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Youlin) A few clicks are all it takes for Xie Peng to virtually traverse his beat in the Qinling Mountains in northwest China's Shaanxi Province. In a control room, the 53-year-old ranger moves his eyes across a three-dimensional map, examining the forest's ridgelines and peering into its ravines. Live footage from drones brings remote stretches of rugged terrain into view. The Fengyu state-owned ecological forest farm, which Xie heads, oversees 215,597 mu of woodland, or nearly 144 square kilometers. Roughly 60 percent of the forest farm's territory lies within the core protection zone of the Qinling Mountains, home to rare and endangered wildlife including giant pandas, golden monkeys and crested ibises. Yet Xie knows this forest in ways no digital map can capture. For almost three decades, he has walked its ridges in mud, snow and summer heat. During this time, he has witnessed not only the forest's recovery, but also a transformation in the work of protecting it. JOB TRANSFORMED When Xie entered the forestry service in 1996, at the age of 23, the mountains were still valued largely for the timber they provided. His first posting was at a timber inspection station near a mountain pass. He spent his days checking trucks carrying logs out of the forest and stopping unauthorized shipments. Two years later, the job began to change. China launched its Natural Forest Protection Program, and Shaanxi Province halted commercial logging in the natural forests of the Qinling Mountains. For Xie and his fellow rangers, the task was no longer to monitor what was being taken out of the mountains, but to safeguard what remained. "From then on, our responsibilities shifted to forest-fire prevention, forest-resource protection and surveys, and the protection of wild animals and plants," Xie recalled. That same year, Xie joined the Communist Party of China (CPC). Over the following decades, ecological conservation in the Qinling Mountains became an increasingly prominent national priority. In 2018, illegal villa construction in the protected areas of the mountains led to disciplinary action against senior provincial and municipal officials, underscoring the importance of protecting the region. A year later, Xie became head of the forest farm and secretary of its Party branch. His responsibilities extended beyond patrolling the mountains himself to leading the team charged with protecting them. LEADING FROM THE FRONT The forest farm currently has 63 employees spread across eight ranger stations, 45 of them CPC members. Three joined the Party after Xie took over in 2019. With the stations scattered across rugged terrain, coordinating the work of the team is no easy task. Xie, notably, did not lead from behind a desk. On patrols that could last eight hours on foot, he made a point of going together with the rangers and often led the way. The Party branch also took its activities deep into the mountains. During one Party Day-themed event, all Party members hiked to a remote section of the forest, each carrying two large bags. They collected plastic bottles and other litter along the trails, then carried the rubbish back down. "I may be the person in charge, but I am a Party member first," he said. "Being a Party member means setting an example through your actions. When the Party branch takes the lead, everyone feels a stronger sense of mission and is more motivated to do their job well." Fire prevention is another regular part of the team's work. The forest farm holds large-scale fire drills every spring and autumn. In the month leading up to each exercise, rangers typically train two or three times a week. Individual outposts also conduct their own drills, preparing groups to respond to possible fires in the areas under their watch. Party meetings, too, sometimes take place in the mountains. With the eight stations scattered across the mountains, rangers cannot always return to the main office after a day in the forest. When they have to stay at an outpost after dark, Xie said, group meetings are held there instead. Concerns raised by frontline rangers are discussed at these meetings and, when necessary, passed on to the authorities. One issue was the harsh conditions at remote stations. Electricity reached the outposts gradually between 2004 and 2012. Before then, rangers relied on candles or kerosene lamps for light and simple coal stoves for warmth. Even after power lines were installed, heating remained inadequate. At the highest stations, winter temperatures can plunge below minus 20 degrees Celsius. As Party secretary, Xie relayed rangers' concerns to local authorities. The district head then traveled up the mountain and spent two hours listening to the workers at a remote station. Shortly afterward, transformers were upgraded and electric boilers installed. "In the past, it was hard for a forest farm like ours to meet the district head or the local Party secretary," Xie said. "Now senior local officials come directly to the mountain stations, listen to our needs, and help resolve practical problems." BEYOND THE SCREEN Work has grown more sophisticated, but has not become any less physical. Xie still makes at least 50 patrols a year, keeps a detailed weekly record of his work, gives up weekends to have joint enforcement operations, and prevents visitors from entering restricted habitats. Technology has given the rangers a wider view of the terrain. Since 2021, the forest farm has gradually built a monitoring system that combines satellite imagery, drones and surveillance cameras. Sixteen high-definition cameras can zoom in and capture images from as far as 20 kilometers away, provided the line of sight is clear. Satellite images are compared each month to detect changes in the forest, while drones survey stretches of terrain difficult to reach on foot. Technology, however, has its limits. Mobile signals often disappear in deep valleys, and cameras cannot see through dense forest canopy. Years of patrolling have made the rangers intimately familiar with their assigned areas. They can often spot changes that a camera might miss. The impact of the rangers' work can be seen in the forest itself. By the end of 2024, the Fengyu forest farm had gone 28 consecutive years without a forest fire. Over the past decade, the team has restored 25,000 mu of forest land and planted more than 280,000 trees. Forest coverage has risen from 78.5 percent to 88.5 percent. Wildlife indicates another sign of the forest's recovery. An infrared camera captured a leopard moving through the undergrowth in August 2022. On June 28, 2025, Xie and his fellow rangers spotted 19 golden takins grazing on a hillside, just over 100 meters away. They kept their distance, careful not to disturb the animals. Nearly three decades after he first stood at a checkpoint inspecting timber trucks, Xie is still walking the ridgelines of the Qinling Mountains. The job has changed and so have his tools. But the goal remains the same: protecting the forest and the life it sustains. "Our mission is to take good care of the forest, let the trees grow, protect wildlife and plants, and allow people and nature to live in harmony," he said. Rangers stage a forest fire emergency drill at the Fengyu state-owned ecological forest farm in Xi'an, northwest China's Shaanxi Province, on Nov. 5, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Youlin)

item.title: Taiwan island fans' invitation to 'Pursuit of Jade' stars to visit the region highlights growing enthusiasm for cross-Straits youth exchanges: Taiwan Affairs Office
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25 12:31:00
Zhang's still in Pursuit of Jade Photo: Courtesy of Douban When asked to comment on the enthusiastic invitation from fans on the island of Taiwan for the two lead actors of Pursuit of Jade , a Chinese mainland costume drama popular in Taiwan region, to visit the island for exchanges, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office said on Wednesday that this was the most vivid demonstration of young people on both sides across the Taiwan Straits reaching out to one another. Zhang Linghe and Tian Xiwei, the lead actors of Pursuit of Jade , recently took part in an online fan meeting for audiences on both sides of the Straits. Many Taiwan local fans enthusiastically expressed their strong desire to invite the two actors to visit the island for exchanges. Both Zhang and Tian said they were eager to visit the island to explore its landscape, experience local life and taste the local delicacies. Zhang Han, a spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said on Wednesday that they have noted the reports, including discussions at the fan meeting about traditional Chinese culture, such as shadow puppetry, Qinqiang opera, flower hairpin adornments and traditional Chinese medicine. Zhang Linghe wrote a calligraphy piece reading "united through drama, together for our shared land," while Tian recalled her university-era visit to the island of Taiwan. Many fans in Taiwan voiced hopes of meeting the two actors in person and looked forward to them visiting soon, according to the spokesperson. "I believe this is the most vivid demonstration of young people on both sides across the Taiwan Straits reaching out to one another. Emotional and cultural resonance serve as a natural bond that brings people across the Straits closer together," Zhang Han said. "We welcome mainland cultural and artistic professionals to engage with audiences on the island and support cross-Straits cooperation in film and television production to create more outstanding works together," Zhang Han added. The Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities' deliberate efforts to obstruct cross-Straits exchanges run counter to public opinion and lack public support, the spokesperson said. Zhang Linghe was previously denied permission to hold an in-person fan meeting in Taiwan region, with the Taiwan's so-called Mainland Affairs Council citing his alleged "demeaning" remarks about the island's status and insufficient details about the event's nature and purpose, the Xinhua News Agency reported. Global Times

item.title: Chinese, Pakistani astronauts achieve first-ever 'space handshake' in China's Tiangong space station
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25 12:02:00
This real-time image captured at Beijing Aerospace Control Center on Nov. 25, 2026 shows China's Shenzhou-24 crewed spaceship docking with the Tiangong space station. China's Shenzhou-24 crewed spaceship successfully docked with the Tiangong space station at 11:56 a.m. (Beijing Time) on Wednesday, according to the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA). The spaceship made a fast, automated rendezvous and docking with the front port of Tiangong's core module Tianhe. The whole docking process took approximately 3.5 hours, said the CMSA. The astronaut trio aboard the spaceship, which comprises Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, Wu Yi and Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreigner to visit Tiangong, will then enter the Tianhe module. The Shenzhou-23 crew members in the space station are ready to receive the new arrivals. (Xinhua/Jin Liwang) China's Tiangong space station welcomed its first-ever "space handshake" between Chinese and foreign astronauts on Wednesday as the Shenzhou-24 crew entered the station, marking a historic moment in China's space history. The Shenzhou-24 crew, comprising Chinese astronaut and mission commander Tang Hongbo, Chinese flight engineer Wu Yi and Pakistani payload specialist Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, entered China's Tiangong space station, where they met with the three Shenzhou-23 astronauts, who have been in orbit for about six months. Ali has made history by becoming the first foreigner to board Tiangong. Chinese President Xi Jinping and Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari exchanged congratulations on Wednesday on the joint spaceflight mission carried out by astronauts from the two countries, according to the Xinhua News Agency. In his message, the Chinese President said the joint space exploration of astronauts from China and Pakistan is a vivid embodiment of the deep-rooted friendship between the two countries, as well as another important achievement in bilateral cooperation. China stands ready to work with Pakistan and other countries to champion the peaceful use of outer space and deepen space cooperation, he said. The mission is a showcase of China's continued technological innovations in the Long March rocket, Shenzhou spacecraft and Tiangong space station, supporting the opening-up and shared use of the China Space Station and multilateral cooperation under China's manned space program, Chinese analysts said. Shenzhou-24 crewed spacecraft ready for launch Photo: Fan Wei /Global Times History made Shenzhou-24 crewed spacecraft and its three-member crew were carried by a Long March-2F Y24 carrier rocket, which lifted off at 8:18 am on Wednesday from Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in Northwest China's Gobi Desert. After entering orbit, the Shenzhou-24 crewed spacecraft successfully docked with the forward port of the space station's Tianhe core module at 11:56 am Beijing time on Wednesday. The Shenzhou-23 crew in orbit opened the hatch of the space station at 2:35 p.m. and welcomed the new arrivals. The entire docking process took approximately 3.5 hours, according to the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA). The two crews then took group pictures of the ninth space get-together in China's aerospace history. They will now start a new in-orbit handover round. After completing a short-term joint flight, Ali will return to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft alongside two Shenzhou-23 crew members. The other two Shenzhou-24 astronauts will stay in orbit for roughly six months along with Shenzhou-23 astronaut Zhu Yangzhu, who has already spent six months in orbit and will remain aboard Tiangong to complete a year-long stay experiment. This was the 8th crewed launch mission since the implementation of the China Space Station application and development program, and the 41st flight mission of China's manned space program. The Long March-2F carrier rocket maintained its stable condition for the high-profile mission. "Although the overall mission plan remained largely unchanged, the rocket team completed 12 technical improvements to further strengthen safety for the flight," Li Wenqing, a technical expert with China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC), told the Global Times. The improvements covered both rocket and ground systems, focusing on reliability, safety redundancy and more efficient launch-site operations. The team optimized the structure and rubber compound formulation of seals in the rocket's pressurization and propellant feed system, while tightening acceptance standards. These improvements enhanced the system's sealing performance, reliability and safety redundancy, Li said. The rocket team also added a manual forced-separation control channel between the rocket and launch tower as a backup for the automatic system, while increasing redundancy in separation signals between systems to improve launch reliability. The movable launch platform also underwent considerable upgrades, including improved displays and human-machine interaction, automatic rotation and speed adjustment, and an upgraded health monitoring system. These changes improved its automation, reliability and operational safety, Li said He Pengju, overall technical lead for launch and tracking operations, told the Global Times that strong winds and sandstorms were more likely during the seasonal transition. The center implemented zoned temperature and humidity controls in the launch area. After the launch, the Long March-2F Y25 carrier rocket will enter emergency rescue standby under the program's rolling backup plan, continuing to support space station missions, the Global Times learned from the launch center. Rapid docking The mission marked the first time a Shenzhou crewed spacecraft carried a foreign astronaut on trip between Earth and space, as well as the first joint flight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts in China's manned space program. The mission represents a major step forward in international cooperation at the China Space Station. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif described Pakistan's participation in the mission as a reflection of living proof of the ironclad friendship, thanking China for making Pakistan part of this historic mission, the prime minister's office said in a X post on Wednesday. Ali, the first foreign astronaut to participate in a Chinese crewed space mission, learned to speak Chinese. Before his departure, he quoted a line from a Chinese poem: "Someday the roc will ride the wind and mount ninety thousand li into the sky." The "roc" refers to an ancient mythical bird and the unit of distance known as a li is equivalent to half a kilometer. Pakistan's Ambassador to China Syed Ali Asad Gillani said in an interview with CCTV News that he was pleasantly surprised by the Pakistani astronaut's proficiency in Chinese. He said Chinese has now become an international language in space. "Learn Chinese well - you never know, it might take you all the way to space!" Li Zhe, an expert at CASC, told the Global Times that the spacecraft and space station teams coordinated closely and made detailed preparations for the Pakistani astronaut's flight. The development team conducted multiple rounds of integrated crew-spacecraft tests involving the primary and backup Shenzhou-24 crews, including the Pakistani astronaut. After arriving at the Jiuquan launch site, the crew took part in spacecraft familiarization and a full-system launch rehearsal, while the space station team provided training on in-orbit living arrangements, equipment operations, experiments and emergency procedures, Li said. The Pakistani astronaut experienced the spacecraft's rapid rendezvous and docking capability. After liftoff, Shenzhou-24 used an autonomous rapid rendezvous and docking mode lasting only about 3.5 hours and successfully docked with the forward port of the space station's Tianhe core module. This marked the fourth time a Shenzhou spacecraft had used the 3.5-hour docking mode. "Unlike radial rendezvous and docking, which requires continuous dynamic adjustments, front-port docking has a stable parking point and is relatively less demanding in terms of flight control," Li said. The 3.5-hour mode is the standard plan, but ground controllers can switch to a five hour or longer docking plan if necessary to ensure the safety of the astronauts, spacecraft and space station. "The value of 3.5-hour rapid rendezvous and docking goes beyond speed," Li said. Early Shenzhou missions took two days and dozens of orbits to complete rendezvous and docking. The faster mode reduces astronauts' physical fatigue and psychological stress during the journey to orbit, while improving the space station's ability to conduct emergency rescue and evacuation. The joint flight with a foreign astronaut and the use of mature rapid rendezvous and docking technology highlight the China Space Station's openness to international cooperation and the continued development of China's manned spaceflight capabilities. Joint space experiments The mission will also feature four scientific experiments carried out by both Chinese and Pakistani astronauts aboard the China Space Station, covering biology, crops and advanced materials. The Pakistani astronaut will operate the experiments in orbit, collecting data for joint research in space. The four experiments focus on cyanobacteria, quinoa, graphene hybrid composites and self-healing carbon fiber composites. Some will be conducted in the life-ecology experiment cabinet in the Wentian lab module, while others will expose materials to the vacuum, radiation and extreme temperature changes outside the space station. "The cyanobacteria experiment aims to explore a potential 'green microfactory' for future deep-space missions," Huang Kun, an expert with the China Space Station's space application system, told the Global Times. Proposed by Pakistan's Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO), the experiment will examine how microgravity and space radiation affect cyanobacteria's photosynthesis, growth and carbon-fixation capacity. The findings could support research into oxygen regeneration and space-based biomanufacturing, Huang said. The quinoa experiment focuses on food security in space. Led by the University of Agriculture Faisalabad (UAF), in Pakistan, it will send 32 quinoa seed samples outside the cabin to study how cosmic radiation and microgravity affect their longevity and nutritional properties. The findings could help identify high-quality varieties for space cultivation and provide reference data for crop breeding on Earth, Huang said. Huang said graphene hybrid composites are lightweight and offer radiation-shielding potential, while self-healing carbon fiber composites are designed to repair microcracks caused by temperature changes, radiation and micrometeoroid impacts, using solar heating outside the cabin to restore their mechanical properties. Both materials experiments will use the space station's external materials exposure facility. The graphene hybrid material will be exposed alongside an aluminum control sample for one year, with detectors recording particle tracks for later comparison of their shielding, mechanical and thermal properties. The self-healing carbon fiber samples, including pre-cracked and intact controls, will be monitored by imaging in orbit and retrieved after one year to assess crack repair, Huang said. With the Pakistani astronaut operating the experiments in orbit, China-Pakistan space cooperation will extend beyond joint spaceflight to the joint design and implementation of scientific experiments.

item.title: Participant in Shanghai hospital's weight-loss competition sheds 16.1 kilograms in three months
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25 11:25:00
Photo: Screenshot from thepaper.cn A participant who initially weighed more than 100 kilograms lost 16.1 kilograms in three months in a weight-loss competition organized by a top-tier Shanghai hospital, reducing body fat mass by 13.6 kilograms and waist circumference by 21 centimeters. His fatty liver disease also improved from severe to mild, thepaper.cn reported. The participant, surnamed Wu, who is 177 centimeters tall, was crowned the competition's overall weight-loss champion, according to the report. According to Shanghai Tenth People's Hospital, which held the competition, a total of 261 participants, with an average age of 36, signed up for the science-based weight-loss competition which opened registration in early May. After three months, 224 participants completed the competition, losing an average of 7.25 kilograms and reducing their waist circumference by an average of 10 centimeters through tailored nutrition, exercise and health management. Bu Le, director of the obesity and metabolic syndrome (weight management) department at the hospital, said more than 70 percent of participants lost at least 5 percent of their body weight, with nearly half shedding at least 10 percent. Most participants also showed improvements in body fat, waist circumference, visceral fat and fatty liver indicators. In addition to Wu, the competition also named champions for the greatest body-fat reduction and waistline slimming. The competition's body-fat reduction champion surnamed Wang, in his 50s, shed 9.4 kilograms in three months, including 9.1 kilograms of body fat. His visceral fat area returned to a normal range while his skeletal muscle mass remained largely unchanged. The competition's waistline reduction champion, surnamed Jiang, lost 14.3 kilograms in three months, including 11.2 kilograms of body fat, and reduced her waist circumference by 24.5 centimeters, the largest reduction among all participants. Her visceral fat area decreased and her metabolic indicators also improved following online training and nutritionist support. According to Bu, the competition prioritized fat loss, muscle preservation, waist reduction and improved metabolic health, with waist circumference and visceral fat considered more meaningful indicators than weight loss alone. Excess visceral fat is closely linked to insulin resistance, fatty liver disease, abnormal blood lipids and cardiovascular diseases and metabolic risks. Global Times

item.title: China successfully launches Shenzhou-24 crewed spaceship with Pakistani astronaut as first foreign guest
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25 08:21:00
The Shenzhou-24 crewed spacecraft carried by the Long March-2F Y24 carrier rocket, lifts off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in Northwest China's Gobi Desert on November 25, 2026. Photo: Fan Wei/Global Times The Shenzhou-24 crewed spacecraft carried by the Long March-2F Y24 carrier rocket lifted off at 8:18 am from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in Northwest China's Gobi Desert on Wednesday, marking China's first crewed spaceflight involving a foreign astronaut. About 10 minutes later, the spacecraft successfully separated from the rocket and entered its preset orbit. The astronauts were in good condition, marking the successful completion of the launch mission. During the mission, the crew will carry out a range of experiments and applications in fields including space life sciences and human research, microgravity physics, and new space technologies. These include multiple scientific experiment projects conducted in cooperation with international partners. To date, a total of 31 Chinese astronauts and one foreign astronaut have made 50 spaceflight trips. The mission also marks the 680th flight of the Long March series of carrier rockets and the 24th flight of the Shenzhou spaceship. The Shenzhou-24 crewed spacecraft carried by the Long March-2F Y24 carrier rocket, lifts off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in Northwest China's Gobi Desert on November 25, 2026. Photo: Fan Wei/Global Times Shenzhou-24 crewed spacecraft ready for launch Photo: Fan Wei /Global Times At a press conference on Tuesday, Zhang Jingbo, spokesperson for the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA), announced that the Shenzhou-24 crew would be led by mission commander Tang Hongbo, Chinese flight engineer Wu Yi and Pakistani payload specialist Muhammad Zeeshan Ali. Tang is set to make his third visit to the China Space Station, while Wu will undertake his first spaceflight. Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali is going to be the first foreign astronaut to visit China Space Station. After entering orbit, the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft is scheduled to use a 3.5-hour autonomous rapid rendezvous and docking strategy, connecting to the forward port of the Tianhe core module to form a three-spacecraft, three-module combination, according to the CMSA. This was the 8th crewed launch mission since the implementation of the China Space Station application and development program, and the 41st flight mission of China's manned space program. The Long March-2F carrier rocket maintained its stable condition for the high-profile mission. "Although the overall mission plan remained largely unchanged, the rocket team completed 12 technical improvements to further strengthen safety for the flight," Li Wenqing, a technical expert with China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC), told the Global Times. The improvements covered both rocket and ground systems, focusing on reliability, safety redundancy and more efficient launch-site operations. The team optimized the structure and rubber compound formulation of seals in the rocket's pressurization and propellant feed system, while tightening acceptance standards. These improvements enhanced the system's sealing performance, reliability and safety redundancy, Li said. The rocket team also added a manual forced-separation control channel between the rocket and launch tower as a backup for the automatic system, while increasing redundancy in separation signals between systems to improve launch reliability. The movable launch platform also underwent considerable upgrades, including improved displays and human-machine interaction, automatic rotation and speed adjustment, and an upgraded health monitoring system. These changes improved its automation, reliability and operational safety, Li said He Pengju, the overall technical lead for launch and tracking operations, told the Global Times that strong winds and sandstorms were more likely during the seasonal transition. The center implemented zoned temperature and humidity controls in the launch area. At a media meeting on Tuesday, Tang recalled the excitement of first entering the China Space Station during the Shenzhou-12 mission five years ago. This time, he said he would welcome an international colleague aboard China's space home. Tang said the joint mission required intensive training in spacecraft operations, emergency response and scientific experiments, while also preparing the crew to support a long-stay astronaut and assist the Pakistani payload specialist. Flight engineer Wu said six months of joint training had enabled the crew to move from simply understanding one another to being able to anticipating each other's actions, despite language and cultural differences. Ali said seven months of training in China had equipped him with flight skills and enabled him to communicate in Chinese with his crewmates. He said he was carrying the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis. After the launch, the Long March-2F Y25 carrier rocket will enter emergency rescue standby under the program's rolling backup plan, continuing to support space station missions, the Global Times learned from the launch center.

item.title: International space cooperation opens a new chapter today: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 22:48:00
China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) on November 24, 2026, unveiled the Shenzhou-24 crew: spacecraft pilot Tang Hongbo (center), flight engineer Wu Yi (right), and payload specialist Muhammad Zeeshan Ali (left). Over the past few decades, the ISS - built and operated primarily by countries including the US and Russia - has been the only "human laboratory" in space, leaving countries of the Global South with virtually no opportunity to even set foot on its threshold. The "Wolf Amendment" enacted by the US also explicitly excluded China from cooperation. Having been denied a "ticket" to the ISS back then, China launched its own space station through self-reliance - and has reserved "seats" for other nations as well. China's Shenzhou-24 crewed spaceship is scheduled to be launched from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center on the morning of November 25, Beijing time. What has drawn significant international attention is the inclusion of the first "non-Chinese face" among the crew for this mission. Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a Pakistani astronaut, will travel to the Tiangong space station alongside Chinese astronauts to complete the first joint flight between Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program. He will also carry out joint China-Pakistan space science experiments. Pakistani media have widely reported on the event, with terms such as a "historic flight" and "the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis" in headlines. Chinese netizens have welcomed the guest with poetic remarks: "Under the starry sky, we greet friends from all quarters; aboard Tiangong, we gather guests from across the globe." A path of cooperation, jointly forged by China and other countries of the Global South, is slowly unfolding in the vast expanse of space. Seven months ago, Ali stepped into the Astronaut Center of China. In his own words, he carries the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis. As is well known, human spaceflight sets extremely high thresholds in terms of industrial infrastructure, scientific research capabilities, and financial investment - thresholds that the vast majority of Global South countries find difficult to overcome on their own. The Outer Space Treaty, which entered into force in 1967, explicitly stipulates that the exploration and use of outer space shall be carried out "for the benefit and in the interests of all countries," irrespective of their degree of economic or scientific development, "without discrimination of any kind." However, over the past few decades, the International Space Station (ISS) - built and operated primarily by countries including the US and Russia - has been the only "human laboratory" in space, leaving countries of the Global South with virtually no opportunity to even set foot on its threshold. Pakistan's first entry into Tiangong is the natural outcome of 36 years of space cooperation between the two countries. As early as 1990, Pakistan's first scientific experimental satellite, Badr-1, was launched aboard a Chinese rocket. Since then, cooperation between the two sides has gradually expanded to fields such as communications, remote sensing, and satellite navigation. In 2024, a Pakistani CubeSat accompanied the Chang'e-6 mission to the Moon, marking the country's first lunar exploration. Now, Pakistan is on the verge of realizing its dream of human spaceflight, and its lunar rover project has been included in the list of international cooperation initiatives for the Chang'e-8 mission. The deepening of China-Pakistan space cooperation serves as a vivid illustration of how collaboration among the Global South is expanding into the frontiers of science and technology. Global South countries not only seek to improve people's livelihoods and advance industrialization but also have the right and the dream to reach the heights of scientific and technological innovation. Looking back on the evolution of China's human spaceflight program, this commitment to openness stands out as all the more precious. China was unable to participate in the construction of the ISS due to external political factors; the "Wolf Amendment" enacted by the US explicitly excluded China from cooperation. Having once stood in the rain ourselves, we are all the more eager to hold an umbrella for others. Before construction began on the Tiangong space station, China extended an invitation for cooperation to the world without any conditions. China, in collaboration with the United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs, selected the first batch of international scientific research projects, involving 23 research institutions from 17 countries. On this mission, Ali will also serve as a payload specialist, carrying out substantive scientific research tasks. Having been denied a "ticket" to the ISS back then, China launched its own space station through self-reliance - and has reserved "seats" for other nations as well. For China's Tiangong space station, this also marks a new beginning, with more countries, particularly those in the Global South, joining hands to build a wider circle of partners. Beyond crewed spaceflight, China has officially presented the United Nations with the first lunar samples collected from the far side of the Moon by the Chang'e-6 mission. The BeiDou Navigation Satellite System provides navigation services to more than 140 countries and regions, while the China-Brazil Earth Resources Satellite program helps protect the Amazon rainforest. China has also signed more than 200 space cooperation agreements with over 50 countries and international organizations. The old era of major powers vying for supremacy in space, which characterized the last century, has come to an end, and a historic new chapter in international space cooperation is unfolding. Outer space has now become a new frontier for human economic and social development. Its exploration and utilization, as well as the formulation of relevant rules, have a direct bearing on the long-term interests of all countries. On October 23, the Chinese side released China's Position on Strengthening Outer Space Governance, explicitly calling for safeguarding the right of all States to have equitable access to outer space and to explore and use it without discrimination, while increasing the representation and voice of developing countries. If the vast majority of Global South countries remain absent from space exploration for an extended period, the power to determine the future allocation of outer space resources and formulate industry rules may once again become firmly concentrated in the hands of a handful of countries. As humanity expands its horizons for survival and development into space, it should not replicate the North-South divide seen on Earth, nor should it allow this new frontier to become the exclusive domain of a few countries seeking to monopolize its benefits. "To see a thousand miles farther, ascend another storey." This line from an ancient Chinese poem was a particular favorite of Ali during his training in China. In the past, people tended to measure progress in space exploration by how far spacecraft could travel and how long astronauts could stay in orbit. Perhaps another yardstick should be added: how many countries have been able to participate in humanity's journey into space, and how many people's dreams have been realized along the way. Outer space is not an exclusive arena for competition among a handful of countries. Every nation with a dream has the right to reach for the stars.

item.title: GT Voice: What Shenzhen means for the Netherlands' chip policy toward China
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 22:34:00
Humanoid robots undergo testing and debugging at Shenzhen's first humanoid robot pilot production line in South China's Guangdong Province on April 12, 2026. Photo: VCG As the global trade environment grows more complex and the US pushes for tighter restrictions on chip exports, Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen's visit to China from Monday to Wednesday has significance beyond diplomacy. He began his trip in Shenzhen, visiting innovative companies and meeting representatives of Dutch businesses. The decision to place business and technological innovation at the center of the visit sends a clear signal of how seriously the Netherlands views economic and technological cooperation with China, as well as opportunities this cooperation offers Dutch businesses. What is happening in Shenzhen? The story is unfolding on two fronts. The first is the city's tech-driven economic growth. In the first 10 months of this year, Shenzhen's foreign trade exceeded 5.25 trillion yuan ($787.8 billion), with imports reaching 2.54 trillion yuan, up 73.7 percent year-on-year. This growth reflects not just demand for foreign goods, but also the expanding industrial activity behind China's technological advances. As a window into China's tech-driven economy, Shenzhen offers foreign businesses more than a market: it offers opportunities to become part of the country's evolving industrial landscape. The second front is technological. China's advances in artificial intelligence (AI) are no longer a matter of aspiration. Just a few months ago, domestically developed AI chips were reported to have successfully supported the full-parameter post-training of a 1.6-trillion-parameter AI model. China's semiconductor industry still has ground to cover, but the progress it has made is increasingly difficult to dismiss. Its growing capabilities are giving China greater strategic leverage in global semiconductors and chipmaking-equipment trade. Whether or not Berendsen's visit brings these broader developments into focus, they are unfolding in the city he chose to visit first. Shenzhen offers a glimpse of an economic reality that the Netherlands cannot afford to overlook. China is not only a vast market for foreign businesses, but also an increasingly capable source of technological innovation. As global technology trade becomes increasingly complex, understanding both dimensions of this development matters for the Netherlands. The two countries' economic ties extend well beyond semiconductors. Their practical cooperation is advancing steadily in fields such as agriculture, water management, environmental protection and science and technology, while people-to-people exchanges continue to deepen. Across these sectors, commercial ties and industrial supply chains are becoming increasingly intertwined, creating benefits for both sides. The growing economic value of this cooperation to the Netherlands deserves greater recognition. The Netherlands has growing economic interests in China, and semiconductors are one area where those interests closely intersect with China's interests. The Netherlands should take China's legitimate concerns over trade in semiconductors and chipmaking equipment seriously and address them through dialogue. A sound approach should take proper account of China's legitimate interests, rather than allow external pressure to dictate the Netherlands' policy. ASML's exports to China have long drawn market attention. Berendsen's visit to Shenzhen and his discussions in Beijing offer an opportunity for the Netherlands to approach the issue more constructively. Exports to China serve ASML's commercial interests and those of the wider Dutch economy. The current political climate in Washington may fuel calls for tighter restrictions on chip exports to China, adding to the pressure on the Netherlands. But US policy calculations do not necessarily align with Dutch economic interests. Cooperation with China brings tangible benefits to Dutch businesses. The Netherlands has good reason to weigh those benefits on their merits, rather than let pressure from Washington dictate its choices. AI is advancing at extraordinary speed, and Shenzhen offers a glimpse of how quickly the technological landscape is evolving. The question for the Netherlands is not simply how to respond to external pressure, but how to retain its place in an industry moving so fast. Pragmatic engagement with China and a willingness to address differences while expanding cooperation would give the Netherlands more room to pursue its own economic and technological interests in a changing world.

item.title: What is China's takeaway from Jensen Huang's saga?
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 12:42:00
Jensen Huang. Photo: VCG Eleven days ago, almost no one would have imagined Jensen Huang walking away from Nvidia. Eleven days later, he was back - in a way few could have predicted - reclaiming his place at the very center of the company's power structure. In the space of just eleven days, certain American media outlets and politicians turned the episode into a Hollywood-style spectacle, complete with gossip, conspiracy theories, and political maneuvering. And then? Huang is back, "posing no national security risk." "Is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the US President said, defending the return. Some Western media outlets spent weeks digging up dirt on him, branding him a "spy," and portraying him as a deeply troubled figure — both personally and professionally. They may be having a hard time explaining what happened next. There he was: Jensen Huang, strolling back into Nvidia headquarters in a dark blue jacket, greeted by cheering employees, a forest of raised phones, and thunderous applause. The Financial Times struck a sour note, casting Huang's return as "a triumph of money over morals." But is that really what happened? Huang's fate was never simply a matter of personal conduct. His future became a pawn in a much bigger game - one involving elections, political infighting, semiconductors, and geopolitics. He made his way back because, after all the political maneuvering and calculations, one thing became clear: The so-called spy allegations, entirely fabricated out of thin air, are nothing more than a political witch hunt; Nvidia and US AI industry still need him. While certain politicians in Washington scramble to carve up the AI compute pie, Silicon Valley's engineers have sent a very different message through their applause: Politics may create enemies, but technological competition is ultimately won through real-world capabilities. You don't win the AI race through political witch hunts or a never-ending expansion of export controls. You win by keeping the people who know how to build, innovate, and deliver. Those invoking "national security" may have plenty to say about GPUs. But the people who actually design and build them know what it takes to stay ahead in the AI race. The Huang episode has also given global markets a fresh and sobering perspective on the relationship between business and government in the US, the country's business climate, and how corporate power really works. In America, the fate of tech companies is never determined by market forces and technological prowess alone. It is deeply intertwined with politics, making even the biggest companies vulnerable to partisan battles, geopolitical rivalries, and political maneuvering. Even for a company as powerful as Nvidia, who really gets to decide something as basic as whether the CEO stays or leaves? After this episode, companies and investors around the world may need to rethink what they thought they knew about doing business in the US, how corporations and government interact, and what corporate independence actually means. Huang is back, but the storm is far from over. More hearings and investigations are on the way and the winds of McCarthyism are still blowing. This farce has shown just how unpredictable and politicized the US business environment has become, and it has given China a clear reminder. Every restriction, political intervention, and so-called national security review Washington has imposed on China's tech industry only reinforces the same lesson: China has no choice but to accelerate its drive for technological self-reliance and build a fully integrated, independent semiconductor supply chain. What is China's takeaway from Jensen Huang's saga? A clearer view of the absurd relationship between American politics and technology - or, more simply, another episode of the American political soap opera.
